# Etiology and Pathogenesis

The scabies mite has four pairs of legs and measures $0.3\mathrm{mm}$ in diameter. It is therefore not easily seen with the naked eye.

<mark>The mite cannot fly or jump; it lives its entire 30-day life cycle in and on the epidermis.</mark> The female mite burrows into the stratum corneum within 20 minutes and lays approximately 3 eggs per day. The eggs hatch after 4 days, and the larvae migrate to the skin surface, where they mature into adults. After 2 weeks, female and male mites copulate, after which the gravid female burrows back into the stratum corneum. The male, which is slightly smaller than the female, falls off the skin and perishes. The average number of mites a host harbors is usually less than 20, except in **crusted scabies** (previously known as Norwegian scabies), in which a host may harbor over a million mites. Individuals with **HIV**, the elderly, and those with medication-induced immunosuppression are at increased risk of developing crusted scabies, although cases have also been reported in immunocompetent individuals, particularly among indigenous Australians.

# Clinical Findings

<mark>After initial exposure to the scabies mite, pruritus and rash may take 6 to 8 weeks to develop.</mark> <mark>With subsequent exposure, symptoms typically appear within a few days due to prior sensitization to mite antigens.</mark> <mark>The itching is severe and often worse at night.</mark> <mark>Lesions present as red, scaly, and sometimes crusted (excoriated) papules and nodules, commonly affecting the:</mark>

- <mark>Interdigital webs</mark>  
- <mark>Sides of the fingers</mark>  
- <mark>Volar aspects of the wrists</mark>  
- <mark>Lateral palms</mark>  
- Elbows  
- Axillae  
- Scrotum  
- Penis  
- Labia  
- <mark>Areolae in women</mark>  

A diffuse erythematous eruption on the trunk may occur as a hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens.

<mark>The **pathognomonic lesion** is a **burrow**—a thin, thread-like, linear structure 1 to $10\mathrm{mm}$ in length—representing a tunnel formed by the mite in the stratum corneum.</mark> <mark>Burrows are most easily seen in the interdigital webs, wrists, or elbows but may be difficult to detect in early disease or after extensive scratching.</mark> To enhance visualization, a black felt-tip marker can be rubbed over the area; after wiping with an alcohol pad, residual ink in the burrow makes it appear darker than surrounding skin.

In infants younger than 2 years, infestation may also involve the **face and scalp**, which are typically spared in older children and adults.

Scabies is transmitted primarily through prolonged close personal contact. However, fomite transmission is possible, as the mite can survive off human skin for up to 3 days.  

## Treatment

Topical scabicides are the preferred treatment. Oral **ivermectin** is an effective alternative, particularly in crusted scabies or when topical therapy is impractical.

## <mark>Identification and Clinical Features of Scabies</mark>

<mark>However, it can be difficult to find burrows in early cases of scabies or after the patient has extensively excoriated the lesions.</mark> <mark>Identification of a burrow can be facilitated by rubbing a black felt-tip marker across an affected area.</mark> After the excess ink is wiped away with an alcohol pad, the burrow appears darker than the surrounding skin due to ink accumulation within it.

<mark>In infants younger than 2 years of age, the face and scalp can be involved, whereas in adults this is rare.</mark> <mark>Erythematous to violaceous pruritic nodules may appear in the axillae and flanks in children, and on the scrotum in men; these are thought to represent a hypersensitivity reaction to the mite.</mark> <mark>Such nodules can persist for weeks after successful eradication of the infection.</mark> <mark>Vesicles and bullae may develop, particularly on the palms and fingers.</mark>

### Crusted Scabies

In crusted scabies, hyperkeratotic plaques develop diffusely on the palms and soles, with nail thickening and dystrophy. The rest of the skin typically appears diffusely xerotic. Pruritus is variable and may be absent. These patients are highly contagious, as their skin may harbor over a million mites, and they can serve as sources of outbreaks in healthcare settings.

## Diagnosis

The definitive diagnosis of scabies is made by microscopic identification of the mite, eggs, or fecal pellets (scybala). This is achieved by placing a drop of mineral oil over a burrow and scraping longitudinally with a number 15 scalpel blade, taking care not to cause bleeding. The collected material is transferred to a glass slide and examined under low-power microscopy.

Other diagnostic methods include:
- **Dermoscopy**, which allows in vivo visualization of the mite (see Chap. 5).
- **Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)** assays that detect mite DNA from skin scales.
- **Skin biopsy**, which may show the mite transected in the stratum corneum.

## Differential Diagnosis

(Refer to Box 208-1 for a list of conditions that may mimic scabies.)

## Complications

Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization) is common and usually responds well to topical or oral antibiotics, depending on the extent of involvement. However, more serious complications such as lymphangitis and septicemia can occur, particularly in crusted scabies. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis has been reported following *Streptococcus pyogenes* pyodermas associated with scabies.

## Prognosis and Clinical Course

If left untreated, scabies can persist for many years. In immunocompromised individuals, the disease may progress to the crusted form, which requires aggressive treatment and infection control measures. With appropriate therapy, the prognosis is excellent, although pruritus and skin lesions may persist for several weeks due to ongoing hypersensitivity.

# <mark>Clinical features</mark>

<mark>Specific manifestations include intense itch and disseminated inflammatory papules.</mark> <mark>Non-specific manifestations which may also occur are skin excoriation, secondary eczematization, and impetiginization.</mark>

## 1. Classical scabies

- <mark>Occurs in patients with normal immune response</mark>  
- <mark>Intense pruritus, worse at night</mark>  
- <mark>Erythematous papules disseminated on the periumbilical area, waist, genitalia, breasts, buttocks, axillary folds, fingers (including interdigital spaces), wrists, and extensor aspects of the limbs. The head, palms, and soles are usually spared in adults</mark>  
- <mark>Papules are small, often excoriated, with haemorrhagic crusts on top</mark>  
- <mark>The burrow (a pathognomonic sign) appears as a thin, brown-grey line of 0.5–1 cm, but is rarely observed due to excoriation or secondary bacterial infection</mark>  
- <mark>Other lesions: vesicles (usually at the start of a burrow), nodules (firm, 0.5 cm in diameter, usually on the male genitalia, groin, buttocks), weals</mark>  
- Poor hygienic conditions may result in secondary bacterial infection  
- Irritant or allergic contact eczema can be induced following topical treatment

## 2. Crusted scabies (the term 'Norwegian scabies' should no longer be used)

- Occurs in patients with severe immune deficiency due to disease (e.g. AIDS, HTLV-1 infection, malignancy, leprosy) or therapy (e.g. immunosuppressant drugs and biologicals), neurological disease causing reduced sensation, immobility with reduced ability to scratch, or in genetically susceptible patients  
- Pruritus is mild or absent  
- Skin lesions consist of generalized, poorly defined, erythematous, fissured plaques covered by scales and crusts. On bony prominences (e.g. finger articulations, elbows, iliac crest), the plaques have a yellow-to-brown, thick, verrucous aspect  
- Diffuse non-crusted scabies with involvement of the back may also occur  
- Bacterial secondary infection can result in malodorous skin lesions

# Diagnosis

<mark>Diagnosis is suspected based on the characteristics of itch (generalized, intense at night), clinical findings, and a suggestive history (e.g.</mark> <mark>exposure context, disease in close contacts).</mark> <mark>Definitive diagnosis is supported by a positive microscopic examination of skin scrapings, which may identify mites, eggs, or faecal pellets (scybala).</mark> <mark>To enhance detection, the burrow can be opened with a fine needle and Müller's oil or immersion oil applied to bring the mite to the surface.</mark> <mark>A negative microscopic result does not exclude scabies.</mark>

<mark>Dermoscopic examination can identify skin burrows and mites (the 'delta' sign at the end of the burrow represents the anterior body of the adult female mite), as well as eggs, and can help guide the site of skin scrapings.</mark> In sexually active patients, STI screening (including HIV test) is recommended.

# General principles of treatment

Ten new clinical trials on scabies treatment have been published since the previous guideline in 2010. Recent data focus on mass population treatment, usually with ivermectin. Based on existing comparative studies on the efficacy of different antiscabetic treatments, a distinction is made only between 'recommended' and 'alternative' treatments. The availability of antiscabetic drugs varies across European countries, leading to variability in treatment choices in practice.

Topical treatment should be applied to all skin areas, including the scalp, groin, navel, external genitalia, finger and toe web spaces, and beneath the nails. It should be applied at night and left in place for 8–12 hours. The skin should be cool and dry before application. A second application is recommended after 7–14 days.

# <mark>Reactions</mark>

<mark>Reactions are part of the natural course of leprosy infection and can be triggered or modified by treatment.</mark> There are three main types: **type I leprosy reaction (T1R)**, also known as **reversal reaction (RR)**; **type II leprosy reaction (T2R)**, also called **erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL)**; and **Lucio's phenomenon**, which occurs specifically in multibacillary patients, particularly in Mexico.

## Type I Leprosy Reaction (T1R)

T1R is a **cell-mediated immunity (CMI) reaction**, classified as a **type IV Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity reaction** directed against *M. leprae* antigenic determinants.  

**Clinical features:**
- Increased inflammation of existing skin lesions: they become more **erythematous, raised, and enlarged**, and may **ulcerate**.
- **Nerve involvement**: nerves may become **inflamed, enlarged, and tender**, leading to:
  - Loss of strength
  - Reduced sensation
  - Decreased sweating
- **Acro-oedema** (swelling of hands and feet)
- Involvement of joints and liver may also occur.

## Type II Leprosy Reaction (T2R)

T2R is primarily an **immune complex-mediated (antigen-antibody) reaction**, affecting tissues such as skin and nerves. However, **cell-mediated immunity and T-cell regulation** also play a role.

**Clinical features:**
- Characteristic **red, painful, tender nodules** in the skin, which may:
  - Ulcerate
  - Resemble erythema multiforme
  - Develop into bullous lesions
- Systemic involvement (multi-organ disease), including:
  - Neuritis
  - Lymphadenitis
  - Orchitis
  - Iridocyclitis
  - Arthritis
  - Hepatitis
- General symptoms: **fever, leucocytosis**, and occasionally **lymphocytes in urine**.

## Treatment of Type I Reaction (T1R)

<mark>The primary treatment is **corticosteroids**:</mark>
- <mark>**Starting dose**: 30–40 mg prednisone daily</mark>
- <mark>**Tapering**: guided by clinical assessments such as:</mark>
  <mark>- Graded sensory testing (e.g., Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments)</mark>
  <mark>- Voluntary muscle testing</mark>
- <mark>**Duration**: 4–12 months</mark>
- <mark>**Minimum effective dose**: 15–20 mg prednisone</mark>
- <mark>**Adequate immune suppression** (>0.25 mg/kg/day) should be maintained for:</mark>
  <mark>- At least **3 months** in borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy</mark>
  <mark>- **6–12 months or longer** in borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy</mark>

## <mark>Recurrence</mark>

After treatment, leprosy may recur due to:
- Undertreatment
- Drug resistance
- Persister organisms
- New infection

Recurrences are generally **sensitive to the original multidrug therapy (MDT)**. However, resistance has been documented to:
- **Dapsone**
- **Rifampicin**
- **Ofloxacin**

Resistance to **clofazimine** has not been convincingly proven.

A **PCR test** is available for detection and monitoring.

### WHO Recommendations for Resistant *M. leprae*

For resistant cases, WHO recommends modifying MDT based on resistance patterns, using a combination of three drugs from the following:
- Ofloxacin
- Clarithromycin
- Minocycline
- Clofazimine

## <mark>Treatment of Type 1 Reaction (T1R)</mark>

<mark>The treatment of Type 1 Reaction (T1R) primarily consists of corticosteroids, starting with **30–40 mg prednisone daily**, tapered gradually over a period of **4–12 months**.</mark> <mark>The tapering should be guided by clinical assessments such as **graded sensory testing** (using Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments) or **voluntary muscle testing**.</mark> <mark>During this period, the dose should remain at least **15–20 mg daily** to maintain effectiveness.</mark>

<mark>Adequate immunosuppression, defined as **>0.25 mg/kg/day**, should be maintained for at least **3 months in borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy**, and for **6–12 months or longer in borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy**.</mark> <mark>In some cases, **dapsone** may help prevent recurrence of reactions.</mark>

<mark>Although the **WHO recommends only 3 months of steroid therapy**, this approach is not widely accepted by most clinicians, who favor longer treatment durations based on clinical response.</mark>

## Treatment of Type 2 Reaction (T2R)

Type 2 Reaction (T2R), often presenting as Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), is more challenging to manage. The reaction is typically **episodic**, with **95% of ENL episodes lasting less than one month**.

- **Mild reactions** can be managed with **NSAIDs**.
- **Arthritis** associated with T2R may respond to **anti-malarial drugs**.

For **severe reactions**, the **WHO recommends**:
> A standard course of **prednisolone** at a dose not exceeding **1 mg/kg/day**, with a total duration of **12 weeks**.

However, clinical experience suggests that **severe reactions often require higher doses (60–120 mg/day)** for a **short duration**, followed by rapid tapering to zero within **one month or less**. Recurrent attacks should be treated similarly. This aggressive short-course approach is not yet universally accepted.

Attempts to **prevent recurrent reactions with prolonged steroid use** are limited by poor efficacy and significant side effects. Since T2R is an **immune complex-mediated reaction**, long-term steroid use often leads to **steroid dependence**, severe adverse effects, and in some cases, death.

Alternative and more effective options include:

- **Clofazimine**: Can prevent or treat T2R.
- **Thalidomide**: Superior to other treatments and effective both therapeutically and as prophylaxis. However, it may not work in all cases.

**Combining low-dose steroids with low-dose thalidomide** is counterproductive and should be avoided.

A major concern with **thalidomide** is its potential to cause **sensory neuropathy**, which can be difficult to distinguish from nerve damage due to leprosy itself.

When **thalidomide is unavailable**, **methotrexate (MTX)**—with or without additional clofazimine—can be considered for preventing recurrent ENL episodes.

## Surgical Intervention

If **nerve function continues to deteriorate despite optimal medical therapy**, **nerve decompression (nerve release) surgery** should be considered.

Surgical evaluation may also be appropriate for **nerves that remain tender after treatment**, even in the absence of an active reaction.

## Lucio’s Phenomenon

Lucio’s phenomenon is a rare, severe form of leprosy reaction seen exclusively in **untreated diffuse lepromatous leprosy**. It presents as **well-demarcated, bizarre-shaped superficial skin ulcers** with **slough (eschar) formation**, resulting from **vasculitis and infarction** due to massive bacillary occlusion of small venules.

It may be triggered by **sudden exposure to cold**.

**Treatment**: Immediate initiation of **Multidrug Therapy (MDT)**, with **rifampicin (RMP)** being the most critical component.

## Management of Leprosy Sequelae

The long-term consequences of leprosy—**sensory loss and muscle weakness**—are the main causes of disability and social stigma.

Management includes:

- Provision of **padded footwear, tools, and utensils** to prevent injury.
- **Tendon transfer surgery** may be considered to improve hand grip or foot function, but only under the guidance of an **experienced physiotherapist**.

**Stigma reduction** is essential and best achieved through **education**, emphasizing that **properly treated patients pose no risk and have minimal complications**.

## Prevention

Despite ongoing research into **DNA-based vaccines**, **BCG vaccination** remains the most effective available prophylaxis in many regions. Protection varies widely—from **<20% to 80%**—likely due to differences in exposure to **environmental mycobacteria**.

The **WHO recommends**:
- A **single 600 mg dose of rifampicin** for **contacts of leprosy patients**, which provides protection for several years.
- **BCG vaccination** may extend this protective effect.

A newer WHO-endorsed strategy involves a **longer initial prophylactic regimen** using **rifampicin in combination with moxifloxacin or clarithromycin** for enhanced and prolonged protection.

## Relapse and Management After Treatment

One group reported relapses beginning 6 years after completion of 2 years of triple drug therapy.[54] Two groups reported relapse after smear negativity had occurred.[54,55] A 1-year course of treatment was associated with a higher relapse rate compared to a 2-year course.[53] These relapses are not considered to be re-infections. There is variation in opinion on how best to manage this issue. The WHO strategy relies on patient self-referral for follow-up. In contrast, USPHS recommendations permit resumption of treatment based on physician evaluation. Another approach is to continue dapsone monotherapy indefinitely after completing multidrug therapy.

## Alternative Antibiotics and Potential Regimens

In addition to rifampin, several antibiotics have potent bactericidal activity against *Mycobacterium leprae*, including minocycline, clarithromycin, and the fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin and levofloxacin). A single-dose regimen of rifampin, ofloxacin, and minocycline is being studied for paucibacillary disease, though the long-term relapse rate remains undetermined.[56] However, daily use of these agents is prohibitively expensive in regions where leprosy is endemic and healthcare resources are limited. It is also unclear whether combinations of these potent bactericidal drugs—though theoretically appealing by analogy to tuberculosis treatment—offer any advantage over current WHO or USPHS guidelines, although they were well tolerated in a small trial.[57]

## Practical Treatment Approach in Multibacillary Leprosy

Given the low incidence of primary dapsone resistance in our multibacillary patient population,[58] we often use a combination of rifampin (600 mg daily) and dapsone (100 mg daily) for 2 to 3 years. After completion of this regimen, the decision to continue dapsone indefinitely or accept an uncertain relapse risk is discussed with the patient.

## <mark>Management of Reversal Reactions</mark>

<mark>In reversal reactions (type 1 reactions), prompt initiation of prednisone therapy is recommended due to the risk of permanent nerve damage.</mark> <mark>The typical starting dose is 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day.</mark> <mark>The dose should be titrated based on nerve tenderness, the patient’s symptoms, and careful sensory assessment of hands and feet—such as with graded Semmes-Weinstein filaments.</mark>

<mark>Prednisone therapy should be tapered slowly, and patients should be informed that treatment may last 6 months or longer.</mark> <mark>If neuritis does not respond promptly to prednisone, rest and splinting of affected extremities are advised.</mark>

### Box 186-2: Medical Management of Reaction States

| Reaction Type | Thalidomide | Prednisone or Prednisolone | Duration | Other Agents of Unproven Value |
|--------------|-----------|----------------------------|--------|------------------------------|
| **Reversal reactions (type 1)** | Of no value | 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day. Rifampin may increase catabolism. Taper slowly. Alternate-day therapy may be well tolerated. | Usually 6 months to 2 years; may vary | Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents |
| **Erythema nodosum leprosum (type II)** | Most effective if available and not contraindicated. Initial dose: 100–200 mg once daily at bedtime. Maintenance: 50 mg every other day to 500 mg daily | Used if thalidomide is unavailable: 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day | Median duration ~5 years; may last up to 10 years | Pentoxifylline |
| **Lucio phenomenon** | Of no value | May be helpful | — | Plasmapheresis reported beneficial in refractory cases |

# <mark>CUTANEOUS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS ASSOCIATED WITH HEMATOLOGIC DISEASES</mark>

## Pallor

<mark>Pallor of the mucocutaneous tissue is most readily observed in the palms, nail beds, face, and conjunctivae—areas where the microvascular bed is visible through the skin.</mark> It results from decreased hemoglobin content.

Multiple factors can cause pallor, including:
- Acute and chronic hemorrhage
- Emotional stress
- Vasopressor drugs
- Cold exposure
- Shock
- Pathophysiologic conditions leading to anemia
- Cutaneous edema

Addressing the underlying cause typically resolves the pallor.

### Anemia

The palmar creases serve as a useful indicator of anemia severity. Normally, they appear pink unless the hemoglobin level falls below the normal range.

Anemia is defined based on the patient’s age and sex. A morphologic classification using red blood cell (RBC) size or volume—assessed via blood smear—helps categorize anemias into:
- **Microcytic** (small RBCs)
- **Normocytic** (normal-sized RBCs)
- **Macrocytic** (large RBCs)

Each type correlates with specific etiologies such as:
- Blood loss
- Genetic disorders
- Decreased RBC production
- Increased RBC destruction

#### Constitutional Signs and Symptoms

Common systemic manifestations of anemia include:
- Malaise
- Fatigue
- Dizziness
- Postural hypotension
- Dyspnea on exertion
- Tachycardia

These symptoms become more pronounced with increased oxygen demand. Red blood cells transport oxygen bound to hemoglobin from the lungs to tissue capillaries. Oxygen release is governed by the characteristics of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.

Laboratory evaluation should be guided by clinical suspicion and typically includes:
- Complete blood count with white blood cell differential
- Iron studies (serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, ferritin)

---

## HEMATOLOGIC DISEASES AT A GLANCE

Mucocutaneous changes—such as pallor, jaundice, flushing, erythema, and cyanosis—can signal underlying hematologic disorders.

Key clinical points:
- Anemia is best classified by mean corpuscular volume (MCV).
- Megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B₁₂ deficiency is distinguished from folate deficiency by the presence of neurologic symptoms (absent in folate deficiency).
- Flushing in carcinoid tumor typically lasts 10 minutes or less; in mastocytosis, it lasts 30 minutes or more.
- Polycythemia vera presents with acrocyanosis, aquagenic pruritus, urticaria, Sweet syndrome, and purpura.
- The morphologic approach to purpura involves the three P's:  
  1. Is the lesion purpuric?  
  2. Is it primary?  
  3. Is it palpable?
- Leukemia cutis refers to localized or disseminated skin infiltration by leukemic cells, indicating systemic disease, dissemination, or relapse.

# <mark>Comparison of guidelines and consensus articles on the management of patients with acne with oral isotretinoin</mark>

## <mark>Abstract</mark>

<mark>Guidelines and consensus statements on the management of acne aim to provide evidence-based, expert-driven recommendations.</mark> This review compares current guidelines and consensus articles to compile recommendations on the use of oral isotretinoin in acne treatment. Ten common and clinically relevant questions are addressed, including indications for isotretinoin, recommended daily and cumulative doses, treatment duration, and laboratory monitoring. Special considerations such as timing of dermatologic procedures and potential associations with depression or inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are also evaluated. A major limitation across guidelines is the use of differing acne classification systems. The recommended daily dose ranges from 0.3 to 0.5 mg/kg in European guidelines to up to 1 mg/kg in U.S. guidelines. Only European guidelines specify a minimum treatment duration of 6 months. <mark>All guidelines emphasize strict pregnancy prevention due to teratogenicity.</mark> Monitoring for symptoms of depression is recommended in European, French, and U.S. guidelines. Key clinical issues that remain inconsistently addressed include age indications, target cumulative dose, timing of procedures, isotretinoin-IBD association, acne flare prevention, and laboratory monitoring protocols. These topics require clearer inclusion in future guidelines, as they frequently arise in clinical practice.

## Introduction

<mark>Oral isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid), a natural metabolite of vitamin A, was approved for the treatment of acne vulgaris in 1982 by the U.S.</mark> <mark>Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and in 1983 by the European Medicines Agency (EMA).</mark> <mark>Isotretinoin undergoes rapid intracellular conversion to all-trans retinoic acid and exhibits strong biological activity with low binding affinity for retinoid receptors.</mark> <mark>It effectively inhibits sebocyte proliferation, differentiation, and lipid synthesis both in vivo and in vitro, reduces *Cutibacterium acnes* (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*) colonization, and decreases inflammation and hyperkeratinization within the pilosebaceous unit.</mark>

<mark>The efficacy and safety of oral isotretinoin were evaluated in a systematic review by Vallerand et al., which included 11 randomized controlled trials published up to 2016.</mark> <mark>All studies demonstrated a clinically significant reduction in acne lesions with isotretinoin compared to control groups (placebo, systemic antibiotics, or other comparators).</mark> <mark>Adverse events occurred approximately twice as often with isotretinoin versus controls.</mark> <mark>Most were cutaneous and related to xerosis.</mark> <mark>Serious adverse events leading to discontinuation included Stevens-Johnson syndrome, severe cheilitis, photophobia, elevated liver enzymes, anorexia, headache, and depression.</mark>

This review compares current international and national guidelines and consensus statements on the use of oral isotretinoin for acne. Guidelines are intended to optimize patient care through evidence-based, critically appraised recommendations on treatment benefits and risks. Key areas of focus include indications for use, dosing strategies (daily and cumulative), treatment duration, laboratory monitoring, and special considerations such as procedural timing and potential psychiatric or gastrointestinal risks.

## Methods

Eligible publications included updated international and national guidelines and consensus articles containing recommendations on oral isotretinoin for acne. EMA recommendations were included as they inform drug prescribing frameworks in Europe. Guidelines published before 2012 or without a stated validity date were excluded. Only publications in English or French were considered.

Search terms included: *isotretinoin*, *systemic treatment*, *acne*, *guidelines*, *consensus*. Reference lists of included articles were manually screened for additional relevant guidelines or consensus documents. The final literature search was conducted on 20 May 2019.

## Myalgias and Musculoskeletal Concerns
Myalgias are the most common musculoskeletal complaint, occurring in 15 percent of patients. In severe cases, creatine phosphokinase levels should be evaluated to assess for possible rhabdomyolysis.

## <mark>Isotretinoin Therapy: Teratogenicity and Contraception</mark>
<mark>The greatest concern during isotretinoin therapy is the risk of administration during pregnancy, which can lead to severe teratogenic effects in the fetus.</mark> <mark>The drug is not mutagenic; its adverse effects occur during organogenesis.</mark> <mark>Therefore, isotretinoin should be reserved for patients who have not responded to other treatments.</mark>

<mark>Women of childbearing age must be fully informed of the risks associated with pregnancy while on isotretinoin.</mark> <mark>Patients must use two highly effective forms of contraception—such as an oral contraceptive combined with condoms and spermicidal jelly—starting at least one month before beginning therapy.</mark> <mark>Female patients must be thoroughly counseled and demonstrate understanding of contraceptive methods prior to treatment initiation.</mark> <mark>Dual contraception must continue throughout isotretinoin therapy and for one month after discontinuation.</mark>

<mark>In the United States, the FDA requires a strict risk management program known as iPledge.</mark> <mark>This computer-based system ensures adherence to pregnancy prevention protocols before, during, and after isotretinoin treatment.</mark>

## <mark>Dosing and Treatment Duration</mark>
<mark>The recommended daily dosage of isotretinoin is 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day.</mark> <mark>A cumulative weight-based dosing target of 120 to 150 mg/kg over the course of therapy is often used, particularly in patients with variable dosing or interrupted treatment, as achieving this total dose improves the likelihood of long-term remission.</mark>

<mark>Patients with severe truncal acne—especially those with back and chest lesions, which respond less robustly than facial lesions—may require higher doses, up to 2 mg/kg/day.</mark> 

<mark>In patients with severe acne, particularly those with granulomatous lesions, disease flares are common at treatment initiation.</mark> <mark>To mitigate this, initial dosing should be low—often below 0.5 mg/kg/day.</mark> <mark>Pre-treatment with prednisone (40 to 60 mg/day) for 1 to 2 weeks may be necessary and sometimes continued for the first two weeks of isotretinoin therapy.</mark>

<mark>A typical course lasts 20 weeks, but duration is flexible.</mark> <mark>Therapy may be extended in patients who do not achieve adequate response.</mark> <mark>Additional improvement may occur for 1 to 2 months after stopping treatment, so complete clearance is not required before discontinuation.</mark>

## <mark>Laboratory Monitoring</mark>
<mark>Baseline laboratory tests should include a complete blood count and liver function tests.</mark> <mark>However, the most critical monitoring involves serum triglyceride levels.</mark>

- <mark>Baseline triglycerides should be measured before starting therapy.</mark>
- <mark>Repeat testing is recommended at 3 to 4 weeks and again at 6 to 8 weeks.</mark>
- <mark>If levels are normal at 6 to 8 weeks and no risk factors are present, further testing may not be needed.</mark>
- <mark>If triglycerides exceed 500 mg/dL, monitoring should be frequent.</mark>
- <mark>Levels above 700–800 mg/dL warrant interruption of therapy or initiation of lipid-lowering treatment.</mark>
- <mark>Complications such as eruptive xanthomas or pancreatitis can occur at very high triglyceride levels.</mark>

## <mark>Diet and Acne</mark>
Several studies have suggested a potential role for diet in acne development. However, the overall evidence remains inconclusive. The impact of chocolate, sweets, milk, and fatty foods on acne requires further investigation. There is no strong evidence supporting routine elimination of these foods. Nevertheless, some patients report disease flares after consuming specific foods—particularly chocolate. Given these individual perceptions, it is reasonable to advise patients to avoid dietary items they believe trigger their acne.

## Acne Surgery
Acne surgery, involving the removal of comedones and superficial pustules, can accelerate the resolution of individual acne lesions. It was historically a mainstay of acne treatment.

# <mark>Part I. Diagnostic confirmation of suspected EB</mark>

## <mark>Diagnosis of EB</mark>

<mark>Providing a precise diagnosis is the first step in approaching a patient suspected of having epidermolysis bullosa (EB) and will yield invaluable prognostic information.</mark> The diagnosis of EB is based on a combination of clinical features, family history, and laboratory findings. Laboratory techniques include immunofluorescence mapping (IFM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and molecular genetic testing. The methods for laboratory diagnosis of EB have been described in detail previously.

### <mark>1. Clinical manifestations</mark>

- <mark>Recurrent blisters and/or erosions of the skin and/or oral mucosa since birth, or starting later in life, induced by mild physical trauma.</mark>  
- <mark>Congenital skin loss.</mark>

**Differential diagnosis** should be excluded based on clinical features and laboratory testing (e.g., microbiologic swabs, histopathology, immunodiagnostics):

- **Neonates**: infections (e.g., staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, multifocal herpes simplex), other genetic disorders with skin fragility or blistering (e.g., epidermolytic ichthyosis), diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis, autoimmune blistering disorders (extremely rare).  
- **Infancy and childhood**: infections, bullous mastocytosis, other genetic disorders with skin fragility, dermatitis artefacta, autoimmune blistering disorders (rare).  
- **Adults**: infections, bullous/erosive adverse drug reactions, autoimmune blistering disorders, dermatitis artefacta.

### 2. Samples for EB laboratory diagnosis (informed consent required)

Whenever possible, laboratory diagnosis should be performed in a specialized EB centre.

- **Genetic testing**: An ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) blood sample (2–5 mL), or alternatively saliva or buccal smear, should be obtained from the patient and, where applicable, both parents.  
- **Skin biopsy**: A 4- to 6-mm punch or superficial shave biopsy from a fresh blister (less than 12 hours old) or induced blister, including perilesional skin, is required. Blisters can be induced by gently rotating a pencil eraser on non-blistered skin.  
  - The biopsy can be stored or immediately shipped in sterile saline, Michel's medium, or frozen for immunofluorescence mapping (IFM). Some laboratories perform immunohistochemistry on formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded tissue.  
  - For transmission electron microscopy (TEM), the biopsy must be placed in appropriate fixative. The diagnostic laboratory should be consulted in advance for specific requirements.  
- **Topical anaesthetic creams** should be avoided, as they may cause artificial epidermal cleavage.  
- When inducing a blister, gently rub intact or perilesional skin.  
- In cases of extreme skin fragility, care must be taken to avoid epidermal detachment or rupture of the blister roof during biopsy.

### 3. Specific tests for EB laboratory diagnosis

- **Genetic testing** is the gold standard, providing a definitive diagnosis and classification of the major EB type and, in many cases, the subtype. It also enables genetic counselling and DNA-based prenatal testing.  
  - A next-generation sequencing (NGS) EB-gene panel is the preferred method, as it includes all known EB-associated genes and ensures comprehensive coverage.  
  - Sanger sequencing may be used when the candidate gene is known and small, or to confirm familial or recurrent variants.  
- The vast majority of EB cases can be genetically characterized using these approaches.

# POSITION STATEMENT

# Practical management of epidermolysis bullosa: consensus clinical position statement from the European Reference Network for Rare Skin Diseases

## Abstract

<mark>Inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB) comprises rare disorders that manifest with fragility and blistering of the skin and mucous membranes, with variable clinical severity.</mark> Management of EB is challenging due to disease rarity and complexity, the wide range of extracutaneous manifestations, and a profound impact on daily life for the patient and family members. Although reference centres providing multidisciplinary care for EB exist in each European country, it is common for healthcare professionals who are not specialized in this rare disorder to treat EB patients. Here, experts of the European Reference Network for Rare and Undiagnosed Skin Diseases (ERN-Skin, https://ern-skin.eu) propose practical recommendations for the diagnosis and management of the most common clinical issues: skin blisters and wounds, oral manifestations, pain, and itch.

## Introduction

<mark>Inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB, ORPHA:79361) represents a group of rare conditions characterized by skin and mucous membrane fragility leading to blister formation.</mark> There are four major types of EB — epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS), junctional EB (JEB), dystrophic EB (DEB), and Kindler EB (KEB) — and over 30 subtypes, each with variable clinical severity.  

The clinical spectrum ranges widely across subtypes. Patients with localized, nonsyndromic forms typically experience blistering mainly on the hands and feet, have normal life expectancy, but may suffer significant impairment in quality of life and daily functioning. In contrast, severe subtypes can be lethal in infancy (e.g., severe JEB) or associated with multiple complications such as sepsis, failure to thrive, severe anemia, and aggressive squamous cell carcinoma, leading to reduced lifespan (e.g., severe recessive DEB [RDEB]).

Despite this heterogeneity, blisters and wounds accompanied by pain and/or itch are common features across nearly all EB subtypes.

Management of EB is complex due to its rarity, clinical variability, and multisystem involvement, which profoundly affect patients and their families. While specialized reference centres offering multidisciplinary care exist across Europe, many patients are often managed by healthcare providers outside these centres who may lack specific expertise in EB.

Comprehensive clinical practice guidelines for various aspects of EB management are available through DEBRA International (https://www.debra-international.org/copy-of-eb-health-care-patient-guid), developed using rigorous methodology based on literature review and expert appraisal. These serve as essential scientific resources.

Recognizing the need for concise, practical guidance, the European Reference Network for Rare and Undiagnosed Skin Diseases (ERN-Skin, https://ern-skin.eu) has developed this position statement to support non-specialist healthcare professionals. The aim is to provide easily implementable recommendations for managing common EB manifestations and emergency situations, enabling rapid decision-making and fostering collaboration between local providers and EB reference centres.

These consensus recommendations were developed by a panel of dermatologists, pediatric dermatologists, and dentists within ERN-Skin. They cover key areas including diagnosis, wound management, oral care, and management of pain and itch.

## Part I. Diagnostic confirmation of suspected EB

### Diagnosis of EB

Establishing a precise diagnosis is the first critical step in managing a patient suspected of having EB, as it provides essential prognostic information and guides long-term care.

The diagnosis of EB is based on a combination of:
- <mark>Clinical findings (distribution and morphology of blisters, nail changes, dental abnormalities, etc.)</mark>
- Family history (including consanguinity and inheritance pattern)
- <mark>Laboratory investigations</mark>

Key diagnostic techniques include:
- <mark>**Immunofluorescence mapping (IFM)**: Identifies the level of skin cleavage and detects abnormalities in structural proteins (e.g., keratins, laminin-332, type VII collagen).</mark>
- <mark>**Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)**: Allows ultrastructural analysis of the dermal–epidermal junction to determine the exact plane of blister formation.</mark>
- <mark>**Molecular genetic testing**: Confirms the diagnosis by identifying pathogenic variants in known EB-associated genes (e.g., *KRT5*, *KRT14*, *LAMB3*, *COL7A1*).</mark>

<mark>These laboratory methods are complementary and should be used sequentially or in parallel depending on clinical urgency and availability.</mark> Genetic testing is essential not only for definitive diagnosis but also for enabling prenatal testing, genetic counselling, and eligibility for emerging targeted therapies.

Early and accurate diagnosis facilitates appropriate multidisciplinary management, improves patient outcomes, and supports informed family planning.

# DNA-Based Prenatal and Pre-Implantation Genetic Testing

**Abbreviations:**  
<mark>EB, epidermolysis bullosa; IFM, immunofluorescence mapping; NGS, next-generation sequencing; TEM, transmission electron microscopy.</mark>

---

- <mark>**Immunofluorescence mapping (IFM)** or immunohistochemistry enables rapid diagnosis, which is critical for determining prognosis in newborns. Severe subtypes of EB—such as severe junctional EB (JEB) or severe recessive dystrophic EB (RDEB)—can be identified based on the level of skin cleavage and the absence or marked reduction of specific proteins.</mark>  
- <mark>In cases with mild skin fragility, IFM and TEM may not provide a definitive diagnosis.</mark>  
- <mark>**Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)** can identify the precise level of skin cleavage and structural abnormalities in keratin intermediate filaments, hemidesmosomes, basement membrane, or anchoring fibrils. It remains useful for early diagnosis in certain EB subtypes, such as severe dominant epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS).</mark>

---

## 4. Delivery of Results

A clinician experienced in EB should communicate the final diagnosis, including the EB subtype, prognosis, and inheritance pattern. <mark>However, even with a confirmed genetic diagnosis, precise prognostic predictions—especially in neonates—may not always be possible.</mark>  

It is essential to:  
- Allow sufficient time for discussion.  
- Involve a psychologist when needed.  
- Provide a translator or cultural mediator, if required.  

Diagnosing EB in neonates presents emotional challenges, particularly in conveying the lifelong, chronic nature of the disease. Explanations may need to be repeated. In severe or lethal forms (e.g., severe JEB), management decisions should consider the family’s social, cultural, and emotional context.  

**Genetic counselling must always be provided.**  
To enable DNA-based prenatal diagnosis in future pregnancies, an EDTA blood sample from the affected infant (index case) should be collected promptly with parental consent—especially in severe, potentially lethal forms.

---

## 5. Prenatal Diagnosis

Once the familial pathogenic variant(s) are identified and parental carrier status is confirmed, **DNA-based prenatal testing** and **pre-implantation genetic testing** can be offered upon request.  

Availability of these tests may vary due to local legal, ethical, and cultural regulations.

---

# Part II. Common Clinical Concerns in EB: Practical Recommendations for Healthcare Providers

## Wound Care in EB

Wound care is the cornerstone of EB management. In the absence of a cure, supportive wound care and early detection and treatment of complications are the mainstays of therapy.

---

### 1. Clinical and Laboratory Assessment

Effective wound care must take into account the following factors:

#### a. EB Subtype and Patient Age  
The severity of mucocutaneous and extracutaneous manifestations, as well as wound characteristics, varies significantly among EB subtypes. These are influenced by:  
- The causative gene  
- Type of mutations  
- Patient age  

An initial assessment should always include:  
- Estimation of body surface area affected  
- Characterization of lesions (blisters, erosions, ulcers, hyperkeratosis)

#### b. Nutritional Status, Chronic Anaemia, and Hypoalbuminaemia  
Malnutrition, chronic anaemia, and hypoalbuminaemia are common—particularly in severe EB subtypes such as JEB and RDEB.  

Contributing factors include:  
- Reduced nutrient intake  
- Chronic inflammation  
- Protein and nutrient loss through extensive, non-healing wounds  

These conditions impair wound healing and must be actively managed.  
- Regular nutritional assessment by a dietitian is essential.  
- In children, monitor growth curves.  
- Routinely check haemoglobin and serum albumin levels.

## Protect Your Skin: Key Recommendations

### Sun exposure can speed up skin ageing  
UV exposure is responsible for about 80% of visible signs of skin ageing, including wrinkles, fine lines, sagging skin, and age spots. Sun-protective habits and regular use of sunscreen can help preserve youthful, healthy skin.

### UV damage adds up over time and can be prevented  
Skin damage from UV radiation accumulates over a lifetime. <mark>UV rays from the sun can cause DNA mutations in skin cells, leading to sunburn, premature ageing, and an increased risk of skin cancer.</mark> Even without sunburn, skin damage can occur. Prevention is essential—and it’s never too late to start protecting your skin, regardless of skin type.

### <mark>Children are especially vulnerable</mark>  
<mark>Unprotected sun exposure during childhood and adolescence significantly increases the risk of skin cancer later in life.</mark> <mark>Encourage sun-safe habits early by using hats, protective clothing, and sunscreen on exposed skin when outdoors.</mark>

---

## How to Protect Your Skin?

The following recommendations summarize effective sun protection strategies.

### Avoid sunbathing  
The World Health Organization classifies ultraviolet (UV) radiation as a proven carcinogen. Sunbathing exposes large areas of skin to harmful UV rays. Using sunscreen during prolonged sun exposure does not fully protect against damage and may lead to longer sun exposure, increasing cancer risk.

### Avoid tanning  
There is no such thing as a "safe" or "healthy" tan. A tan is a sign that your skin is trying to protect itself from UV damage—it is an SOS response.

### Avoid tanning beds  
Tanning beds emit intense UV radiation and are proven to increase the risk of all types of skin cancer, especially when used at a young age. They also accelerate skin ageing.

### Protect skin when UV index is 3 or higher  
The UV index measures the strength of UV radiation, ranging from 0 (low) to 11+ (extreme). When the index reaches 3 or above, sun protection is necessary to prevent skin damage.

### Avoid the sun at midday  
UV radiation is strongest 2 hours before and after solar noon (when the sun is highest in the sky). Plan outdoor activities outside this window when possible. If you must be outdoors during peak UV times, use protective measures.

### Use shade and protective clothing  
Seek shade whenever possible, especially around midday. Wear:
- A wide-brimmed hat  
- Long-sleeved shirts and long pants  
- Sunglasses with UVA and UVB protection  
Tightly woven fabrics offer the best defense.

### Use sunscreen on uncovered skin  
When the UV index is 3 or higher, apply broad-spectrum sunscreen with:
- SPF 30 to 50+ (protects against UVB)  
- UVA protection (look for the UVA label)  
Apply sunscreen before going outside and reapply at least every 2 hours, or more often after swimming, sweating, or towel drying.

### Monitor your skin: Watch that SPOT!  
Check your skin regularly for:
- New growths  
- Changes in moles (size, shape, color)  
- Sores that don’t heal  
See a dermatologist or GP if you notice any of these signs. Early detection of skin cancer greatly improves treatment outcomes.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does consistent UV protection cause vitamin D deficiency?  
Sun-safe behavior as recommended does not typically cause vitamin D deficiency in individuals with fair skin who are active outdoors. Most people can maintain adequate vitamin D levels through incidental sun exposure and diet. If vitamin D levels are a concern, consult a healthcare provider about testing or supplementation.

# <mark>ULTRAVIOLET RADIATION</mark>

<mark>UVR represents approximately 5 percent of terrestrial solar radiation and is officially divided into UVA (315 to 400 nm), UVB (280 to 315 nm), and UVC (100 to 280 nm), though other definitions are widely used (e.g., a UVB/UVA division at 320 nm).</mark> <mark>UVA is sometimes subdivided into UVAI (340 to 400 nm) and UVAII (315/320 to 340 nm).</mark> Sealevel solar UVR is approximately 95 percent to 98 percent UVA and 2 percent to 5 percent UVB. <mark>UVC is completely absorbed by stratospheric ozone ($\mathrm{O}_3$) that also attenuates UVB.</mark> <mark>A given solar UVR spectrum varies with the solar zenith angle (the angle between an imaginary perpendicular line and a line from its base to the sun), which is dependent on time of day, season, and latitude.</mark> <mark>The highest UVB content is found when the sun is directly overhead with the shortest path (e.g., noon at the equator at high altitude).</mark>

# Measurement of Human Exposure to Ultraviolet Radiation

The measurement of UVR exposure is called dosimetry and can be done physically or biologically. Accurate physical dosimetry, in which dose rate (irradiance) is measured as $\mathrm{W/cm}^2$ and exposure dose as $\mathrm{J/cm}^2$ [$\mathrm{W/cm}^2$ × time (seconds)], is technically demanding, and a biologic approach is more commonly used. This is based on the individual minimal erythemal dose (MED), which is the lowest dose required to produce a just perceptible erythema (sunburn) 24 hours later. In general, individuals with higher skin types have higher MEDs. However, there is considerable MED overlap between skin phototypes.

Most human UVR exposure is from sunlight, but the use of tanning devices is increasingly popular. Solar UVR exposure may be intentional or inadvertent and depends on specific behaviors and time spent outdoors, as well as photoprotection strategies.

# ACUTE AND CHRONIC EFFECTS OF ULTRAVIOLET RADIATION ON THE SKIN

## AT A GLANCE

- Acute and chronic responses to ultraviolet radiation (UVR) depend on skin phototype.  
- The major acute clinical effects are inflammation, tanning, and immunomodulation.  
- Basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, and photoaging are the chronic effects of UVR.  
- The majority of effects of solar UVR on the skin are the result of its small UVB content.

# Action Spectroscopy

In any skin response to UVR, it is important to know which wavelengths are primarily responsible. This relationship is known as the action spectrum and is fundamentally based on the UVR-absorbing properties of the molecule (chromophore) that initiates the effect (see Chap. 88).

# <mark>Major Features and Complications of Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

## <mark>Clinical Features of Acute Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

- <mark>**Fever**</mark>  
- <mark>**Acute multisystem vasculitis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Polymorphous exanthem**</mark>  
- <mark>**Bilateral bulbar nonexudative conjunctival injection**</mark>  
- <mark>**Inflammation of the oropharynx**</mark>  
- <mark>**Erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or periungual desquamation**</mark>  
- <mark>**Acute non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy** (≥1.5 cm in diameter)</mark>

## <mark>Complications of Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

- <mark>**Coronary artery abnormalities**, including aneurysms</mark>  
- <mark>**Myocarditis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Arthralgia and arthritis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Urethritis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Aseptic meningitis**</mark>

<mark>Prompt treatment with **intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)** and **aspirin (ASA)** significantly reduces the risk of coronary artery abnormalities.</mark>

## Epidemiology

Nationwide epidemics with wave-like spread occurred in Japan in **1979, 1982**, and **late 1985 to early 1986**. Since the mid-1980s, the incidence of Kawasaki syndrome (KS) in Japan has steadily increased, with the **1998 incidence more than 1.5 times higher than in 1987**. The endemic annual incidence is approximately **111 per 100,000 children under 5 years of age**.

Both endemic and epidemic cases in Japan occur most frequently in **late winter and spring**, with a smaller peak in **late fall**. KS is increasingly recognized in other Asian countries. In **Taiwan (1966–2002)**, the annual incidence was **146 per 100,000**, with a peak during **summer months**.

In the **United States and Europe**, KS occurs **sporadically** or as **community-wide outbreaks**. The highest U.S. incidence is reported in **Hawaii** (hospitalization rate: **47.7 per 100,000 children <5 years**). In the continental U.S., incidence ranges from **9 to 19 per 100,000**.

- **Peak age**: 18 to 24 months  
- **>80% of cases** occur in children **<5 years**, with most under **2 years**  
- **Infants <12 months**, especially those **<6 months**, are at higher risk for coronary artery abnormalities  
- **Prevalence by race**: Highest in **Asians**, intermediate in **Blacks**, lowest in **Whites**  
- **Clinical presentation** is similar across all racial groups  

Although **antecedent respiratory illness** and **exposure to rug cleaning** have been associated with KS, neither has been consistently confirmed as a risk factor.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis

Substantial evidence supports **immune activation** as a central mechanism in Kawasaki syndrome:

1. **Activated immune cells**: The acute phase features increased numbers of **activated helper T cells**, **monocyte/macrophages**, and **polyclonal B-cell activation**.  
2. **Proinflammatory cytokines**: Elevated serum levels of **IL-1**, **TNF-α**, **IL-6**, **adrenomedullin**, and **vascular endothelial growth factor** correlate with the development of coronary artery abnormalities.  
3. **Histopathology**: Vascular lesions in medium-sized arteries suggest **immune-mediated injury**.  
4. **Autoantibodies**: Circulating antibodies cytotoxic to **cardiac myosin** and **IL-1/TNF-α/IFN-γ-stimulated endothelial cells** are present.  
5. **Response to therapy**: **IVIG plus aspirin** reduces immune activation; **aspirin alone** does not.

Despite these findings, the **exact etiology remains unknown**. KS is hypothesized to result from an **abnormal immune response to an infectious trigger**, supported by:

- Acute, self-limited course  
- Seasonal and geographic clustering  
- Predilection for young children  

Extensive investigations (serologic, culture, molecular) have **failed to identify a consistent causative agent**. At one time, a **novel human coronavirus** was suspected, but this has not been confirmed.

# HISTORICAL ASPECTS

Kawasaki syndrome (KS), originally called mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, was first recognized and described in Japan in 1967 by Dr. Tomisaku Kawasaki. He reported his experience with 50 children who had been seen during the preceding 6-year period at the Tokyo Red Cross Medical Center. These children appeared to manifest a constellation of findings distinct from any previously described disease. After this description, numerous cases were reported throughout Japan. Dr. Kawasaki's first description of the disease in the English language appeared in 1974. In 1976, the syndrome was first reported in the United States by Melish, Hicks, and Larson in a group of 12 children from Honolulu seen between 1971 and 1973. Since then, KS has been recognized worldwide in children of every racial group. The Kawasaki Disease Research Committee published the fifth revised edition of its diagnostic guidelines in 2005.

# EPIDEMIOLOGY

Although Kawasaki syndrome occurs worldwide in children of all racial groups, it is most prevalent in Japan and in children of Japanese ancestry. KS is primarily an illness of young children, with approximately 80% of patients younger than 5 years of age. The male-to-female ratio is about 1.5:1. The incidence rate is highest among Japanese children between 6 and 12 months of age, with similar numbers affected in the first and second years of life. Secondary cases rarely occur in the same school, daycare center, or household, suggesting that person-to-person transmission is unlikely. In Japan, the recurrence rate of KS is reported to be 3.9%, and the proportion of sibling cases is 1.4%. In patients whose parents had KS in childhood (0.2% of over 32,000 cases), there is a higher rate of sibling cases, increased likelihood of recurrence, greater need for intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and more coronary abnormalities one month after onset. The rate of recurrence is highest within the first 12 months after the initial episode. These findings suggest a common exposure to an infectious agent in genetically predisposed individuals.

The incidence of KS in Japan increased from 1967 to the mid-1980s.

# KAWASAKI SYNDROME

## AT A GLANCE

Most common cause of acquired heart disease in children, with highest prevalence in those of Japanese ancestry.

### Major Features of Acute Kawasaki Syndrome

- Fever
- Acute multisystem vasculitis
- Polymorphous exanthem
- Bilateral bulbar nonexudative conjunctival injection
- Inflammation of the oropharynx
- Extremity changes: erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or periungual desquamation
- <mark>Acute non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm in diameter)</mark>

### <mark>Diagnostic Criteria for Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

Fever lasting 5 or more days without another explanation, plus at least four of the following five criteria:

- Bilateral painless bulbar nonexudative conjunctival injection  
- Changes in the oropharynx: injected or fissured lips, injected pharynx, or strawberry tongue  
- Extremity changes: erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or periungual desquamation  
- Polymorphous exanthem  
- Acute non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm in diameter)

> **Note:** A diagnosis of atypical Kawasaki syndrome may be made in patients with fever and fewer than four criteria if coronary artery aneurysms are present.

### Complications of Kawasaki Syndrome

- <mark>Coronary artery abnormalities, including aneurysms</mark>  
- Myocarditis  
- Arthralgia and arthritis  
- Urethritis  
- Aseptic meningitis  

### Treatment

Prompt treatment with **intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)** and **aspirin** significantly reduces the risk of coronary artery abnormalities.

## <mark>Stage 3 and Stage 4 of Kawasaki Syndrome (KS)</mark>

<mark>In stage 3 (28 to 31 days), the acute inflammatory process regresses, and granulation tissue forms in the coronary arteries.</mark> <mark>In stage 4 (40 days to 4 years), scar formation, organization of thrombi, intimal proliferation, and neoangiogenesis continue for several years after disease onset.</mark> These changes can lead to severe stenosis of the coronary arteries and other medium-sized arteries.

Although coronary arteries are invariably involved in KS, nearly any medium- or large-sized blood vessel may be affected, as observed at autopsy. Aneurysms have been reported in the femoral, iliac, renal, axillary, and brachial arteries. KS is a systemic vasculitis that primarily affects small- and medium-sized blood vessels. However, cutaneous vasculitis is not a prominent feature.

## Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis

According to the American Heart Association guidelines, the diagnosis of KS requires:

- Fever lasting ≥5 days without another explanation, **and**
- At least four of the following five criteria:
  1. Bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection  
  2. Mucous membrane changes (e.g., cracked or injected lips, diffuse oral/pharyngeal erythema, or "strawberry tongue")  
  3. Peripheral extremity changes (e.g., palm/sole erythema, hand/foot edema in acute phase, or periungual desquamation in convalescent phase)  
  4. Polymorphous exanthem  
  5. Acute non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy (>1.5 cm in diameter)

In **incomplete KS**, the diagnosis is considered in patients with fever ≥5 days and fewer than four criteria, especially when coronary artery abnormalities are detected by two-dimensional echocardiography or coronary angiography. In some cases with prominent clinical features, treatment may be initiated before day 5 of fever.

**IVIG and aspirin (ASA)** should be started as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.

### Incomplete KS

- Most commonly seen in infants <6 months of age, particularly males
- Defined as fever ≥5 days with **at least two** principal clinical criteria
- No other plausible explanation for the illness
- Laboratory findings resemble those of classic KS (e.g., elevated acute phase reactants)
- High risk of coronary artery abnormalities

The diagnosis should be considered in any infant with unexplained fever ≥5 days, even with only one clinical criterion.

**Findings that suggest an alternative diagnosis** include:
- Discrete intraoral ulcers
- Exudative conjunctivitis
- Generalized lymphadenopathy (rare in acute KS)

### Differential Diagnosis

KS shares clinical features with infections, hypersensitivity reactions, and environmental toxin exposure. Its mucocutaneous manifestations overlap with other conditions, making differential diagnosis challenging.

A site-specific differential diagnostic approach is useful. The diagnosis relies on recognizing the **cumulative pattern** of mucocutaneous, systemic, and laboratory findings.

Factors that help exclude other conditions:
- Measles, influenza: consider local epidemiology, vaccination status, and culture results
- Adenovirus infection: can mimic KS, especially in young children

Diagnostic uncertainty may arise in atypical cases that do not meet full criteria but develop coronary artery abnormalities.

Support for initiating treatment in borderline cases may include:
- Elevated acute phase reactants (e.g., WBC, ESR)
- Pericardial effusion on ultrasound
- Anterior uveitis on slit-lamp examination

## Treatment

The goal of treatment is to:
- Reduce inflammation in the myocardium and coronary artery walls
- Prevent coronary thrombosis

**Standard therapy** for nearly 20 years has been the combination of:
- **Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)**
- **Aspirin (ASA)**

# <mark>Tertiary Syphilis</mark>

- **Gummatous syphilis**: Characterized by granulomatous lesions (gummas) presenting as nodules, plaques, or ulcers affecting the skin, mucous membranes, and visceral organs.
- **Late neurosyphilis**: Includes a range of neurological manifestations that may occur years after initial infection:
  - Meningeal involvement (chronic meningitis)
  - Cranial nerve dysfunction
  - Meningovascular syphilis (can lead to stroke or myelitis)
  - Parenchymatous neurosyphilis:
    - General paresis (dementia, psychiatric symptoms)
    - Tabes dorsalis (sensory ataxia, lightning pains, areflexia, bladder dysfunction)
- **Cardiovascular syphilis**: Typically manifests decades after infection:
  - Aortic regurgitation
  - Stenosis of coronary ostia
  - Thoracic aortic aneurysm (especially of the ascending aorta)

> **Note**: Neurological involvement in syphilis can occur at any stage—early (e.g., during secondary syphilis) or late (tertiary syphilis).

---

# <mark>Laboratory Diagnosis</mark>

## <mark>Demonstration of *Treponema pallidum*</mark>

<mark>Direct detection methods provide definitive diagnosis of syphilis.</mark>

- <mark>**Darkfield examination (DFE)**:</mark>
  <mark>- Historically the gold standard for diagnosing primary syphilis via visualization of motile spirochetes in fluid from chancres or erosive skin lesions.</mark>
  <mark>- Offers immediate results but is labor-intensive, operator-dependent, and prone to false-negative (common) and false-positive (less common) results.</mark>
  <mark>- Not recommended for routine use due to the availability of more sensitive and specific molecular methods.</mark>

- <mark>**Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)**:</mark>
  <mark>- Preferred method for direct detection, especially for oral, genital, and cutaneous lesions where contamination with non-pathogenic treponemes may occur.</mark>
  <mark>- Can be performed on lesion exudate, tissue biopsies, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and blood (though blood PCR is insensitive).</mark>
  <mark>- No internationally standardized assay exists; therefore, laboratories must use rigorously validated, quality-controlled PCR protocols.</mark>

- <mark>**Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**:</mark>
  <mark>- Uses polyclonal antibodies against *T. pallidum* to detect treponemes in fixed tissue sections (skin, mucosa, organ biopsies).</mark>
  <mark>- Useful in histopathological confirmation but not suitable for routine clinical diagnosis.</mark>

- <mark>**Hybridization techniques**:</mark>
  <mark>- Not used in routine diagnostics due to complexity and limited availability.</mark>

- <mark>**Warthin-Starry (argentic) staining**:</mark>
  <mark>- Difficult to perform and interpret; low sensitivity and specificity.</mark>
  <mark>- Rarely useful in clinical practice.</mark>

- <mark>**Direct fluorescent antibody test (DFA)**:</mark>
  <mark>- Requires specialized equipment, reagents, and training.</mark>
  <mark>- Not recommended for routine diagnosis.</mark>

- <mark>**Molecular epidemiological typing**:</mark>
  <mark>- Techniques include PCR, PCR-RFLP, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), and whole genome sequencing.</mark>
  - Limited by the high genetic conservation of *T. pallidum* genome, resulting in low discriminatory power among strains.

---

## Serological Tests for Syphilis (STS)

Serological testing remains essential for the presumptive diagnosis of syphilis.

- **Important limitation**: STS cannot differentiate between venereal syphilis (*T. pallidum* subsp. *pallidum*) and non-venereal treponematoses:
  - Yaws (*T. pallidum* subsp. *pertenue*)
  - Bejel (endemic syphilis; *T. pallidum* subsp. *endemicum*)
  - Pinta (*T. carateum*)
- These organisms are morphologically and antigenically similar. Differentiation relies on clinical presentation, epidemiology, mode of transmission, and genomic sequencing.

> **Clinical implication**: A reactive STS should be managed as syphilis unless there is documented evidence of prior adequate treatment (Grade 1, Level D recommendation).

### Non-treponemal tests (NTT)

- Detect antibodies (IgG and IgM) against cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen complexes (so-called "reagin" tests).
- Examples:
  - Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test
  - Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) test
  - Toluidine Red Unheated Serum Test (TRUST)
- Advantages:
  - Inexpensive, simple to perform, and widely available.
  - Useful for monitoring disease activity and treatment response (titers correlate with disease activity).
- Seroconversion:
  - Typically occurs 10–15 days after appearance of the primary chancre (~6 weeks post-infection).
- Natural history:
  - Titers peak 1–2 years after infection.
  - Remain detectable at low levels even in late, untreated syphilis.
  - Spontaneous seroreversion (conversion to negative) is extremely rare in tertiary syphilis.

## Clinical Diagnosis of Leprosy

<mark>Skin lesions in leprosy are typically hypopigmented or erythematous macules, papules, nodules, or plaques, which may be skin-colored or slightly red.</mark> <mark>Clinically, leprosy is diagnosed when a patient presents with at least two of the three cardinal signs.</mark> <mark>However, the WHO considers a single cardinal sign sufficient for diagnosis in endemic areas, often overlooking nerve enlargement.</mark>

### The Three Cardinal Signs of Leprosy (Known for Over 100 Years):

1. <mark>**Loss of sensation in a skin lesion**</mark>  
2. <mark>**Enlarged peripheral nerve**</mark>  
3. <mark>**Positive skin smears**</mark>

To date, there are no definitive laboratory tests to diagnose leprosy. <mark>Available tests support classification, monitoring, and detection of relapse but are not diagnostic on their own.</mark>

---

### <mark>1. Loss of Sensation</mark>

<mark>Loss of sensation is assessed using a wisp of cotton wool.</mark> <mark>The lesion is touched—**not brushed**—while the patient’s eyes are closed.</mark> <mark>The patient indicates where they feel the touch.</mark> <mark>To confirm accuracy, sensation is also tested in the skin surrounding the lesion (Fig.</mark> 2).

Alternative sensory tests include:
- <mark>Testing for warm and cold perception</mark>
- <mark>Assessing diminished sweating (e.g., iodide starch test)</mark>
- <mark>Histamine test on the affected area compared with normal skin (evaluates axonal reflex)</mark>

These tests assess damage to dermal nerves. <mark>Notably, leprosy primarily affects the nervous system, making it fundamentally a **neural disease of the skin**.</mark>

---

### 2. Enlarged Peripheral Nerves

<mark>Enlarged nerves may involve:</mark>
- <mark>Cutaneous nerves</mark>
- <mark>Subcutaneous nerves near skin lesions</mark>
- <mark>Major nerve trunks</mark>

Key nerves to palpate include:
- <mark>Posterior auricular nerves</mark>
- <mark>Ulnar nerves</mark>
- <mark>Radicutaneous nerves</mark>
- <mark>Median nerves</mark>
- <mark>Lateral popliteal nerves</mark>
- <mark>Posterior tibial nerves</mark>

<mark>Assessment should include evaluation of:</mark>
- Nerve thickness
- <mark>Consistency</mark>
- Tenderness (Fig. 3a,b)

Ultrasound is a valuable tool for assessing nerve enlargement.

<mark>It is important to note that enlarged fasciculi within the nerve may present a characteristic diagnostic pattern.</mark> Clinicians should also check for sensory loss or muscle weakness in the distribution of the affected nerve, although these signs may not always be apparent. Nerve conduction studies can provide additional diagnostic support.

---

### 3. Skin Smears for Acid-Fast Bacilli

<mark>Smears are collected from:</mark>
- Earlobes and other cooler body areas
- <mark>The **edge of the lesion** in paucibacillary (PB) patients</mark>
- <mark>The **center of the lesion** in multibacillary (MB) patients</mark>

<mark>Technique:</mark>
- Squeeze the skin to reduce bleeding and numb the area
- <mark>Make a small incision into the dermis</mark>
- Collect tissue fluid only—**blood dilutes the sample** and reduces bacillary concentration

<mark>Bacilli are quantified using:</mark>
- **Bacillary Index (BI):** Logarithmic scale for bacilli count
- **Morphological Index (MI):** Percentage of intact (viable) bacilli

#### Staining Considerations:
- <mark>Use **1% hydrochloric acid in isopropyl alcohol** for decolorization (as in Fite stain)</mark>
- Avoid **3% hydrochloric acid** (used in Ziehl-Neelsen stain for TB), as *M. leprae* is less acid-fast than *M. tuberculosis*
- Using 3% acid may result in false-negative smears

#### Molecular Detection:
- <mark>PCR and NASBA can detect *M. leprae* DNA/RNA</mark>
- <mark>However, these methods are often negative in PB patients</mark>
- Smears, immunological assays, and molecular techniques are most useful in diagnosing MB leprosy, monitoring treatment, and detecting relapse

---

### Additional Laboratory Investigations

Other laboratory tests may support the diagnosis but are **not universally diagnostic** across the spectrum of leprosy. No single test confirms leprosy in all cases. <mark>Clinical evaluation remains paramount.</mark>
